summary.text: Working in the \(p\)-adics, the proof writes the successive binomial ratios as products \(F(1)\) and \(F(2)\); pairing each index \(j\) with \(p^{v+1}-j\) turns \(F(t)^2\) into a product in \(t^2+t\), whose second-order expansion is controlled by inductive divisibility of reciprocal-square and reciprocal-fourth-power sums (reduced modulo \(p\)). Substitution into the target difference then cancels the low-order terms, using \(\binom{2p^v}{p^v}\equiv2\) and \(\binom{3p^v}{p^v}\equiv3\pmod{p^3}\) for \(p\ge5\), together with the corresponding weaker congruences at \(p=3\), leaving a multiple of the required power of \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\ge 3\) and every \(r\ge 2\),
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]

We work in the ring \(\mathbb Z_p\) of \(p\)-adic integers. Divisibility by powers of \(p\) in this ring will be written in the usual way. Every ordinary integer embeds in \(\mathbb Z_p\), and for an integer \(m\), divisibility of its image by \(p^k\) is equivalent to ordinary integer divisibility \(p^k\mid m\). Thus it is enough to establish the desired divisibility in \(\mathbb Z_p\).

For \(m\) divisible by \(p\), set
\[
J(p,m)=\{j:0\le j<m,\ p\nmid j\}.
\]
If \(j\in J(p,m)\), then \(j\) is a unit in \(\mathbb Z_p\); write
\[
y_j=\frac1j\in\mathbb Z_p.
\]

We first record an elementary product expansion that will be used below. If each member \(w_i\) of a finite family is divisible by \(q\), then
\[
\prod_i(1+uw_i)-1
\]
is divisible by \(q\), and
\[
\prod_i(1+uw_i)-1-u\sum_iw_i
\]
is divisible by \(q^2\). More precisely,
\[
q^3\mid
2\left(\prod_i(1+uw_i)-1-u\sum_iw_i\right)
-u^2\left(\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^2-\sum_iw_i^2\right).
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, upon expanding the product, the constant, linear, and quadratic terms are
\[
1,\qquad u\sum_iw_i,\qquad u^2\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^2-\sum_iw_i^2=2\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j.
\]
After the displayed subtraction, only terms containing at least three of the \(w_i\)'s remain, and all are divisible by \(q^3\). This argument does not require division by \(2\).

Fix from now on a prime \(p\ge3\). For \(v\ge0\), put
\[
N=p^{v+1},\qquad J_v=J(p,N),
\]
and define, for \(t,u\in\mathbb Z_p\),
\[
F_v(t)=\prod_{j\in J_v}\left(1+tN y_j\right),
\tag{2}
\]
\[
z_j=N^2y_jy_{N-j},\qquad
G_v(u)=\prod_{j\in J_v}(1+uz_j).
\tag{3}
\]
The reflection \(j\mapsto N-j\) permutes \(J_v\). Since
\[
jy_j=1,\qquad (N-j)y_{N-j}=1,
\]
we have
\[
y_j+y_{N-j}=Ny_jy_{N-j}.
\tag{4}
\]
Pairing one copy of \(F_v(t)\) with the reflected copy gives, factor by factor,
\[
(1+tNy_j)(1+tNy_{N-j})
=1+(t^2+t)N^2y_jy_{N-j}.
\]
Consequently
\[
F_v(t)^2=G_v(t^2+t).
\tag{5}
\]

We next relate \(F_v\) to binomial coefficients. Splitting a factorial product into factors divisible by \(p\) and factors prime to \(p\) gives the following identity. For nonnegative integers \(c',n\),
\[
\binom{p(c'+n)}{pn}\prod_{j\in J(p,pn)}j
= inom{c'+n}{n}\prod_{j\in J(p,pn)}(pc'+j).
\tag{6}
\]
To see this directly, begin with
\[
\binom{p(c'+n)}{pn}(pn)!=\prod_{k=1}^{pn}(pc'+k).
\]
Among \(1,\dots,pn\), the multiples of \(p\) are \(p,2p,\dots,np\). On both sides, separate these multiples from the nonmultiples of \(p\). The multiples contribute \(p^n n!\) on the factorial side and
\[
p^n\prod_{i=1}^n(c'+i)
=p^n n!\binom{c'+n}{n}
\]
on the other side. Cancelling the nonzero common factor \(p^n n!\) yields (6).

Take \(c'=tp^v\), \(n=p^v\), so that \(pn=N\). In \(\mathbb Z_p\), all \(j\in J_v\) can be inverted, and (6) becomes
\[
\binom{(t+1)p^{v+1}}{p^{v+1}}
= inom{(t+1)p^v}{p^v}F_v(t).
\tag{7}
\]
Define
\[
B_{2,v}=\binom{2p^v}{p^v},\qquad
B_{3,v}=\binom{3p^v}{p^v}.
\]
Then (7), with \(t=1,2\), gives
\[
B_{2,v+1}=B_{2,v}F_v(1),
\qquad
B_{3,v+1}=B_{3,v}F_v(2).
\tag{8}
\]

We now establish the needed bounds on reciprocal power sums. Put
\[
P_{2,v}=\sum_{j\in J_v}y_j^2.
\]
For \(w\in\{0,1\}\), the following induction principle holds:
\[
p^{v+w}\mid P_{2,v}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p^{v+1+w}\mid P_{2,v+1}.
\tag{9}
\]
To prove it, write \(M=p^{v+1}\). The elements prime to \(p\) below \(pM\) are uniquely \(Mt+i\), where \(0\le t<p\) and \(i\in J(p,M)\). A direct calculation from
\((Mt+i)y_{Mt+i}=iy_i=1\) gives
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{p-1}y_{Mt+i}^{2}
=py_i^2-M\sum_{t=0}^{p-1}t\,y_i y_{Mt+i}(y_{Mt+i}+y_i).
\tag{10}
\]
After summing over \(i\), the first term is \(pP_{2,v}\), which has the required divisibility by the hypothesis in (9). If \(w=0\), the second term is already divisible by \(M=p^{v+1}\), which suffices. If \(w=1\), reduce its remaining sum modulo \(p\). Since \(M\equiv0\pmod p\), we have
\[
y_{Mt+i}\equiv y_i\pmod p,
\]
so, for fixed \(i\), the factor apart from \(t\) is independent of \(t\) modulo \(p\). But for odd \(p\),
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{p-1}t=\frac{p(p-1)}2\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Thus the remaining sum is divisible by \(p\), and the second term in (10) is divisible by \(Mp=p^{v+2}\). This proves (9).

There are two useful initial versions of this bound. The version with \(w=0\) starts trivially at \(v=0\), so for every odd prime,
\[
p^v\mid P_{2,v}.
\tag{11}
\]
If \(p\ge5\), there is an extra factor. Modulo \(p\), inversion permutes \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), and hence
\[
P_{2,0}\equiv\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}x^2=0\pmod p.
\]
Here the last equality is the standard finite-field power-sum identity
\(\sum_xx^k=0\) for \(0<k<p-1\); it applies to \(k=2\) because \(p\ge5\). Applying (9) with \(w=1\) therefore gives
\[
p^{v+1}\mid P_{2,v}\qquad(p\ge5).
\tag{12}
\]

We will also need a fourth-power bound, but only for \(v\ge1\):
\[
p\mid\sum_{j\in J_v}y_j^4.
\tag{13}
\]
Indeed, split the range below \(p^{v+1}=p\cdot p^v\) into the \(p\) blocks \(p^vt+i\). Because \(v\ge1\), reduction modulo \(p\) gives
\(y_{p^vt+i}\equiv y_i\), independently of \(t\). Thus every residue contribution occurs \(p\) times and the sum is zero modulo \(p\).

Introduce the sums
\[
Z_v=\sum_{j\in J_v}z_j,
\qquad
W_v=\sum_{j\in J_v}z_j^2,
\qquad
U_v=\sum_{j\in J_v}(y_jy_{N-j})^2.
\]
From (4), after multiplying by \(y_j\), one obtains
\[
y_jy_{N-j}=-y_j^2+Ny_j^2y_{N-j}.
\]
Therefore
\[
Z_v=N^2\left(-P_{2,v}+N\sum_{j\in J_v}y_j^2y_{N-j}\right).
\tag{14}
\]
If \(w\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p^{v+w}\mid P_{2,v}\), then \(N=p^{v+1}\) is also divisible by \(p^{v+w}\). It follows from (14) that
\[
p^{3v+2+w}\mid Z_v.
\tag{15}
\]
Also,
\[
W_v=N^4U_v.
\tag{16}
\]
Modulo \(p\), since \(N-j\equiv-j\),
\[
(y_jy_{N-j})^2\equiv y_j^4.
\]
Thus (13) implies \(p\mid U_v\) for \(v\ge1\), and (16) gives
\[
p^{4v+5}\mid W_v\qquad(v\ge1).
\tag{17}
\]
Without using (13), (16) always gives the weaker bound
\[
p^{4(v+1)}\mid W_v.
\tag{18}
\]

Apply the product expansion (1) to \(G_v(u)\). Each \(z_j=N^2y_jy_{N-j}\) is divisible by \(N^2=p^{2(v+1)}\). Hence
\[
p^{6(v+1)}\mid
2\bigl(G_v(u)-1-uZ_v\bigr)
-u^2(Z_v^2-W_v).
\tag{19}
\]
This is the second-order approximation to \(G_v\).

We next derive a strong bound for \(F_v(t)-1\). Suppose \(w\in\{0,1\}\) and
\(p^{v+w}\mid P_{2,v}\). Then
\[
p^{3v+2+w}\mid F_v(t)-1
\qquad(t\in\mathbb Z_p).
\tag{20}
\]
First, directly from (2), every nonconstant term in the product is divisible by \(N\), so
\[
p^{v+1}\mid \varepsilon,
\qquad \varepsilon:=F_v(t)-1.
\tag{21}
\]
By (5), with \(u=t^2+t\),
\[
G_v(u)-1=2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2.
\tag{22}
\]
Substitute (22) into (19). The terms involving \(Z_v\) are divisible by \(p^{3v+2+w}\) by (15). The term \(Z_v^2\) has at least that divisibility, as does \(W_v\) by (18); and the error modulus \(p^{6(v+1)}\) is also at least as large. We conclude that
\[
p^{3v+2+w}\mid 2(2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2).
\tag{23}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, \(2\) and \(4\) are units in \(\mathbb Z_p\). Initially, (21) makes \(\varepsilon^2\) divisible by \(p^{2(v+1)}\). Because \(3v+2+w\ge2(v+1)\), the identity
\[
4\varepsilon=2(2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2)-2\varepsilon^2
\]
first improves (21) to
\[
p^{2(v+1)}\mid\varepsilon.
\]
Now \(\varepsilon^2\) is divisible by \(p^{4(v+1)}\), and
\[
4(v+1)\ge3v+2+w
\]
for \(w\le1\). Applying the same identity once more to (23) proves (20).

We need two elementary consequences for the binomial coefficients. If \(p\ge5\), use (12) and (20) with \(w=1\). From (8), induction beginning with
\(B_{2,0}=2\), \(B_{3,0}=3\) gives
\[
B_{2,v}\equiv2\pmod{p^3},
\qquad
B_{3,v}\equiv3\pmod{p^3}
\quad(p\ge5).
\tag{24}
\]
Indeed, at each step \(F_v(1)-1\) and \(F_v(2)-1\) are divisible by
\(p^{3v+3}\), hence in particular by \(p^3\).

For \(p=3\), the weaker direct estimate (21), together with (8), gives
\[
B_{2,v}\equiv2\pmod3,
\qquad
B_{3,v}\equiv3\pmod9.
\tag{25}
\]
The first congruence follows immediately by induction. For the second, assume it at stage \(v\). Then \(3\mid B_{3,v}\), while \(3\mid F_v(2)-1\); consequently
\[
B_{3,v+1}-B_{3,v}=B_{3,v}(F_v(2)-1)
\]
is divisible by \(9\). The initial value is \(B_{3,0}=3\), so (25) follows.

We now prove the main one-step congruence. Let \(v\ge1\), and set
\[
A_v=B_{3,v}^2-27B_{2,v}.
\]
Choose \(w=1\) when \(p\ge5\), and \(w=0\) when \(p=3\). In either case we have
\[
p^{v+w}\mid P_{2,v}.
\tag{26}
\]
We also claim
\[
p^{4-w}\mid 12(2B_{3,v}^2-9B_{2,v}).
\tag{27}
\]
For \(p\ge5\), write from (24)
\[
B_{3,v}=3+p^3k,\qquad B_{2,v}=2+p^3m.
\]
Then
\[
2B_{3,v}^2-9B_{2,v}
=p^3\bigl(2k(B_{3,v}+3)-9m\bigr),
\]
which proves (27) with \(w=1\). For \(p=3\), write from (25)
\[
B_{3,v}=3+9k,\qquad B_{2,v}=2+3m.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
2B_{3,v}^2-9B_{2,v}=27(4k+6k^2-m).
\]
Multiplication by \(12\), which itself is divisible by \(3\), proves divisibility by \(3^4\), namely (27) with \(w=0\).

For brevity write \(F_1=F_v(1)\), \(F_2=F_v(2)\). By (5),
\[
F_1^2=G_v(2),\qquad F_2^2=G_v(6).
\tag{28}
\]
Using (8), (28), and the second-order expression (19) for \(G_v(2)\) and \(G_v(6)\), straightforward expansion yields the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
4(A_{v+1}-A_v)
={}&Z_v\,12(2B_{3,v}^2-9B_{2,v})\\
&+(Z_v^2-W_v)(72B_{3,v}^2-108B_{2,v})\\
&+2B_{3,v}^2\Bigl(2(G_v(6)-1-6Z_v)-6^2(Z_v^2-W_v)\Bigr)\\
&-27B_{2,v}\Bigl(2(G_v(2)-1-2Z_v)-2^2(Z_v^2-W_v)\Bigr)\\
&+54B_{2,v}(F_v(1)-1)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{29}
\]
For completeness, this identity is obtained by replacing
\(A_{v+1}\) with \(B_{3,v}^2F_2^2-27B_{2,v}F_1\), replacing the squares \(F_2^2,F_1^2\) according to (28), and adding and subtracting the linear terms \(uZ_v\) and quadratic terms \(u^2(Z_v^2-W_v)/2\) for \(u=6,2\). The final term arises because \(G_v(2)=F_1^2=1+2(F_1-1)+(F_1-1)^2\). Thus (29) is purely an algebraic rearrangement.

Every term on the right side of (29) is divisible by \(p^{3v+6}\). For the first term, (15) and (27) give
\[
(3v+2+w)+(4-w)=3v+6.
\]
For the second, \(Z_v^2\) has more than enough divisibility by (15), while \(W_v\) is divisible by \(p^{4v+5}\) by (17), and
\(4v+5\ge3v+6\) because \(v\ge1\). The third and fourth terms are divisible by \(p^{6(v+1)}\) by (19), and
\(6(v+1)\ge3v+6\). Finally, (20) says that \(F_v(1)-1\) is divisible by \(p^{3v+2+w}\), so its square is again more than sufficiently divisible. Since \(4\) is a unit for odd \(p\), (29) therefore proves
\[
p^{3v+6}\mid A_{v+1}-A_v
\qquad(v\ge1).
\tag{30}
\]

Finally let \(r\ge2\) and put \(v=r-1\), so \(v\ge1\). By definition,
\[
A_v=a(p^v),\qquad A_{v+1}=a(p^{v+1}).
\]
Also
\[
3v+6=3(r-1)+6=3r+3.
\]
Thus (30) says
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1}),
\]
which is exactly
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}.
\]
This proves the conjecture for every prime \(p\ge3\) and every integer \(r\ge2\).
